web_evidence.note: On his official site, Sparks explicitly contrasts The Choice's complete third-person narration with The Notebook being written in both first and third person.

web_evidence.title: Excerpt from The Notebook by Nicholas Sparks
web_evidence.note: Publisher-authorized Chapter One excerpt sustains Noah's participating I narration as he prepares to read the notebook.

web_evidence.title: The Notebook — Official PDF Excerpt
web_evidence.note: The author-hosted extended excerpt from the 1946 narrative sustains external he narration and access to Noah's memories and thoughts.

web_evidence.title: CliffsNotes on Nicholas Sparks' The Notebook
web_evidence.note: Wiley's structural analysis states that Noah narrates the opening and closing chapters, while the middle chapters use limited third-person omniscient narration.

web_evidence.note: Its point-of-view entry independently describes alternation between Noah's first-person nursing-home account and limited third-person retrospectives focused on Noah and Allie.

search_log: Searched "The Notebook" "Nicholas Sparks" with excerpt, first chapter, point of view, narrator, frame narrative, first person, and third person terms.

Opened the publisher-authorized BookBrowse Chapter One excerpt and the author-hosted 37-page PDF excerpt; these established first-person opening narration and sustained third-person interior narration respectively.
Searched Nicholas Sparks's official site for structural comments and found his explicit whole-book statement that The Notebook uses both first and third person.
Opened Wiley/CliffsNotes and LitCharts structural analyses to verify that the shift is sectional: first-person opening and closing frame chapters surround third-person middle chapters.
Checked Google Books and general author-page synopsis results, but their preview or synopsis material did not independently establish the complete person structure.
person_note: The novel has sustained base narration in two grammatical persons. Noah narrates the present-day nursing-home frame in first person in the opening and closing portions, while the long 1946 notebook/reunion story is narrated in limited or omniscient third person. The diagnostic quotes contain both frame-narrator I passages and sustained external he/she passages, matching the authorized excerpts and explicit structural sources. Dialogue, letters, maxims, and poetry are local material and do not create additional base strands. The remaining uncertainty is limited to the attribution of a few isolated quote fragments, not the whole-book structure.
